Indifference is the state of having no interest, concern, or feeling about something or someone. It means something simply does not matter to you — not in a good way, not in a bad way — just not at all.

Think of it as a blank space where a feeling should be. When you are indifferent to something, your reaction to it is essentially: "So what?"
The Key Idea: The Absence of Feeling

This is the most important thing to understand about indifference — it is not a feeling itself. It is the absence of feeling.

Consider these three reactions to rain:

  • A farmer worries about too much rain — that is concern.
  • A child loves rain and wants to splash in puddles — that is joy.
  • An office worker stares out the window at the rain and feels... nothing. It does not affect their mood at all. They neither like it nor dislike it. — That is indifference.

The office worker is not pretending not to care. They genuinely do not care. The rain registers in their mind but lands nowhere in their heart.

Because indifference lives in a quiet, neutral space, it is easy to confuse it with things it resembles but is fundamentally different from.

Indifference is not hatred. If you hate something, you feel strongly against it. Hatred is a burning, active emotion. Indifference is cold and still. Hatred pays attention; indifference looks away.

Indifference is not dislike. Dislike is a mild negative feeling — you prefer something not to exist or happen. Indifference has no preference at all.

Indifference is not tolerance. Tolerance means you do notice something and find it uncomfortable or disagreeable, but you allow it. Indifference means it barely registers.

Indifference is not peace or acceptance. A monk who has found peace has worked through his feelings and arrived at a calm place. An indifferent person never had feelings about the matter to begin with — or has completely disconnected from them.

Indifference is not shyness or silence. A quiet person may care very deeply but simply not speak. An indifferent person may speak freely — but what they say reveals they have no stake in the matter.

If emotions had temperatures, love and hate would both be hot — one warmly, one scorchingly. Indifference is ice cold — or perhaps more accurately, it has no temperature at all.

This is why indifference can sometimes feel more painful to receive than hatred. If someone hates you, at least they are thinking about you. Their hatred shows you matter enough to provoke a reaction. But if someone is indifferent to you, you are essentially invisible to them. You do not even earn a reaction.

This is captured beautifully in a famous idea by Holocaust survivor and writer Elie Wiesel: "The opposite of love is not hate, it is indifference." Hate is love's dark mirror — both are forms of passionate attention. Indifference is love's true opposite, because it offers nothing at all.

Indifference is not always total. It exists on a spectrum.

At its mildest, indifference is simply a lack of enthusiasm or investment. Someone asks you, "Do you want pizza or pasta?" and you say, "Either is fine with me." You have a slight indifference to the choice. This is sometimes called being neutral or impartial.

At its moderate level, indifference means something genuinely does not concern or affect you. You hear that a sports team you have never followed lost a match. You think, "Okay," and move on. No interest is sparked. No feeling is stirred.

At its deepest level, indifference is a profound emotional detachment — even toward things that most people would strongly care about. A person who shows no concern for another person's suffering or pain, even when they could easily help, is displaying deep indifference. At this level, indifference becomes a serious moral issue.

Indifference is not always a flaw. In certain situations, it is a genuine strength.

Indifference to criticism — when you are confident and grounded in your work, the negative opinions of others do not shake you. This indifference protects your focus and mental peace.

Indifference to peer pressure — when others try to push you into doing something you do not want to do, being genuinely indifferent to their approval means they have no power over you.

Indifference to outcomes you cannot control — great philosophers and thinkers (especially the Stoics) taught that learning to feel indifference toward things outside your control is a path to freedom and calm. If the weather will be bad regardless of how much you worry, becoming indifferent to it saves you unnecessary suffering.

In these cases, indifference is essentially a form of emotional freedom — the ability to remain unaffected by things that do not deserve your energy.

Indifference becomes a serious problem when it appears in situations where care, empathy, or responsibility are expected.

Indifference to suffering is widely considered one of the worst human failures. If a person is in pain and you have the power to help but feel nothing — no pull toward them, no discomfort at their situation — your indifference enables harm to continue.

Indifference in relationships is devastating. In a friendship, marriage, or family bond, one person's indifference to the other's feelings, needs, or presence slowly destroys the relationship. It says, wordlessly: "You don't matter to me."

Indifference to injustice means staying silent and unbothered when something wrong is happening. It makes the problem worse by removing any chance of resistance or change.

This is why indifference — especially collective indifference — has historically allowed great wrongs to persist.
How the Word Is Used (Grammar & Phrasing)

The noun indifference is almost always followed by the prepositions "to" or "toward."

  • Indifference to something: "her indifference to money"
  • Indifference toward someone: "his indifference toward his neighbors"

You will commonly see it paired with these kinds of words:

  • Show indifference — "He showed complete indifference to the news."
  • Display indifference — "The crowd displayed indifference to the speaker."
  • Treat with indifference — "She treated their complaints with indifference."
  • Cold indifference — emphasizes the chilling, emotionless quality.
  • Studied indifference — this is a special phrase meaning someone is deliberately performing indifference — they actually do care, but they are pretending not to, usually to seem cool or unaffected.
  • Shrug of indifference — a physical gesture that embodies the feeling.

These sentences show how the word behaves in real use:

"The company's indifference to its workers' complaints eventually led to a strike."
→ The company showed no concern for the complaints. They did not respond, fight back, or engage — they simply did not care.

"What struck her most about him was not his cruelty, but his indifference — he did not even notice how much he had hurt her."
→ He felt nothing about the harm he caused. That emptiness was more painful than if he had acted with intention.

"A good scientist must develop an indifference to what they *want to be true, and care only about what is true."*
→ Here, indifference is positive — the scientist must not let personal wishes cloud their judgment.

"He greeted both praise and criticism with the same indifference — neither moved him."
→ He was emotionally steady and unaffected by outside opinions.

"The indifference of passersby while the man collapsed on the street was deeply disturbing."
→ People saw something terrible and felt nothing strongly enough to act. Collective moral failure through absence of feeling.
One Final Way to Lock It In

If you ever need to recall the precise meaning of indifference, ask yourself this simple question:

"Does this person care — even a little — in any direction?"

If the answer is no — no love, no hate, no worry, no excitement, no concern — what you are looking at is indifference. It is the human equivalent of a blank wall where a window should be. Something that should open up onto feeling simply doesn't.

That is indifference — complete, exact, and in full.
